# CHECKS

1. Costume recognisability — for each costumed character, name any garment that breaks this: Every garment is one that costume is known for, named with the word that names it there. A garment that only hints at the theme does not count, and neither does one borrowed from a different costume or named with a word belonging to one.

3. Colour distinction — name any two characters whose largest garment shares a dominant colour. Name any colour that breaks this: Every colour is one of these words, alone: red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, brown, black, white, grey. 4. Slot conflicts — name any character whose outfit breaks this: One state per garment slot: never two garments in one slot that exclude each other, and a slot the character does not wear is omitted, never written out as empty.
5. Face — name any garment that breaks this: No garment covers the face or the eyes, or shadows them with a brim: no mask, visor, veil, helmet, crown or low brim. Glasses are identity, not a garment: a character whose outfit lists glasses keeps them, and every rewrite of that outfit still lists them.
6. Completeness — name any character whose outfit is missing a top, a bottom or footwear. An outfit that replaces the legs (a tail, a fin, a fused lower body) needs no bottom or footwear; it breaks this: A costume that replaces the legs (a tail, a fin) is one tail from the waist down, written as replacing the legs. Never a skirt over legs, and no feet, bare feet or footwear. Rewrite such an outfit as one tail from the waist down replacing the legs. A `nightwear` outfit needs a top and a bottom but no footwear: slippers, socks or bare feet are all complete.
7. Style world — only when a world is named below. Name any character wearing nothing from that world, and any character whose whole outfit has been replaced by it rather than accented.
8. Sex — name any character whose outfit breaks this: A male character wears garments made for boys or men, a female character garments made for girls or women. When a costume has a male and a female form, each character wears the form matching theirs. Replace the garment with that character's form of it, never by removing the slot.
9. Coverage — name any character listed under `Characters:` whom a page costumes or transforms (a tail, wings, an animal form, a disguise) and whose wardrobe has no category covering that appearance. Add the missing entry under the heading `## <CharacterName> / costumed:<costume>` with the full outfit describing the transformed or costumed appearance. Also name any character a page puts in bed, or into pyjamas for a bedtime routine at night (an adult in bed included, an adult who only sits at a bedside excluded), whose wardrobe has no `nightwear` entry. Add it under the heading `## <CharacterName> / nightwear` with the full pyjama outfit. Nightwear is two-piece pyjamas: a top covering the torso from shoulders to waist (long or short sleeve) and pyjama bottoms (long or shorts). Slippers or socks may be worn, or bare feet. Never a vest or singlet, a bare chest or midriff, or a one-piece or nightdress. Animals, creatures and other figures of the plan have no wardrobe here; never add one.
10. Child coverage — name any child whose outfit breaks this: A child's swimwear, costume or nightwear always has a covering top: a long-sleeve or short-sleeve `swim shirt` (rash-guard) over the whole torso, shoulders to waist (nightwear: the pyjama top the nightwear rule defines). Never a `bikini`, a bare chest, a bare midriff, or a one-piece (a skirt or tail below it leaves the torso reading bare). A child's `nightwear` outfit breaks it too when it breaks this: Nightwear is two-piece pyjamas: a top covering the torso from shoulders to waist (long or short sleeve) and pyjama bottoms (long or shorts). Slippers or socks may be worn, or bare feet. Never a vest or singlet, a bare chest or midriff, or a one-piece or nightdress.
11. Garment variety — name any two characters who break this: Two characters never wear the same set of garments recoloured, neither the whole outfit nor what is left once a page takes an outer layer off. A child's covering top and a leg-replacing tail are never the garment given up: vary colour, sleeve length, neckline and trim around them. Rewrite one with different garment types and silhouette; the story world decides the wardrobe.
12. Plot garments — name any garment the page plan uses as an object (held, lent, wrapped, lost) that no outfit names, or that the outfit names as a different garment. Rewrite the outfit of the character who wears it first (the one the plan first gives it to, when no one wears it) so it wears that garment, described as worn — never when, where or to whom it is lent or taken off. A garment belongs to ONE outfit: that of the character who wears it first. When the plan hands it to another character — to hold, wrap, wear or keep — the plan line and that page's `wornItems` row carry the handoff; the receiver's outfit never names it. No two outfits name the same garment. A garment another character's outfit already names is never added to a second outfit, whoever the plan hands it to. Name any garment two outfits both name, and rewrite the outfit of the character who does not wear it first without it.
13. Appearance only — An outfit `description` is appearance only: garments, colours, materials, fastenings. No page numbers, no events, no other character or creature, no carried item or what a pocket holds. A garment a page takes off stays in the outfit as worn; the `wornItems` row of that page records it off, never the outfit. Name any outfit that carries more, and rewrite it as the appearance alone.
14. Props — A garment is clothing a person wears: coat, scarf, hat, cloak, boots. A blanket, towel, sheet, tablecloth, bag, umbrella, toy, tool or any other object that is carried, held, spread out, shared or wrapped around someone for a page is a story prop, never a garment: no outfit names it, however the plan uses it. The plan line and the Visual Bible carry a prop. Name any outfit that lists a prop, and rewrite it without it.

Fixing check 1 outranks fixing check 3: a character in the right costume sharing a colour with someone else is better than a distinct colour on a garment that does not read as the costume. Two characters of different age or sex may wear the same headwear.

A rewrite must not create a fault of its own. Before writing a corrected outfit, check it against every other character's outfit — including the ones you are leaving alone — and against the outfit you are replacing. Swapping two colours between characters leaves them as hard to tell apart as before.

A row for every garment `description` names, and none for anything it does not.

5. Face: "Coral tiara" — a tiara is a form of crown. Crowns sit on the head and can shadow the eyes or read as obstructing the face area; the rule says no crown. This breaks the face check.
6. Completeness: The mermaid costume replaces the legs; it needs a tail from the waist down, not a skirt. The current outfit has a top and a skirt but no tail, making it an incomplete mermaid costume. 8. Sex: Lily is female, and the garments listed are consistent with girls' wear. No male-character conflicts exist.
9. Coverage: Lily has the costumed appearance (mermaid) covered, though it needs rewriting. Page 4 places Lily in bed in a darkened holiday flat, clearly a bedtime/night scene. She needs a nightwear outfit added.
10. Child coverage: Lily is 6. A child's mermaid tail replaces the legs; the top must provide full torso coverage. Nightwear must be two-piece pyjamas.
11. Garment variety: Only one character exists; no variety conflict.
12. Plot garments: The shell bracelet is a key plot object (Mia's bracelet that Lily knocks into the water and later retrieves). Mia is mentioned in the page plan but has no wardrobe entry; the bracelet belongs to Mia, who wears it first. Lily's current outfit lists a "shell necklace" — this is a different garment. Alternatively, if Mia is not a main character requiring a full wardrobe, the bracelet as a plot garment worn by Mia must appear somewhere. Rewrite the outfit of the character who wears it first so it wears that garment." This implies Mia needs an outfit. The Characters list only names Lily, but the page plan clearly features Mia as a character wearing the bracelet. I will add Mia's outfit under a new heading.
13. Appearance only: The current outfit description is appearance-only, no events or page numbers mentioned. It passes.
14. Props: The shell necklace could be read as a prop if it's a necklace Mia lost, but Lily's outfit lists it as an accessory she wears — a shell necklace is a garment. No props listed as garments in the current entry.

Additional issues from Checks: The costume needs to be a mermaid tail replacing the legs. The top must be a swim shirt for child coverage. The tiara must be removed (face check). The colour "sea green" must become a single-word colour — green or blue. I'll use "green" for the top, as mermaid costumes typically suggest ocean hues. The shell necklace remains as an accessory.

Mia needs an outfit for the plot garment (shell bracelet) and because she appears in the page plan. Her outfit will be a play outfit for a 6-year-old girl at the lake in autumn — perhaps a top, shorts or skirt, and the shell bracelet as an accessory.
